# Sources, Sinks, and Input Formatters {#sec-sources-sinks}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A stream processing engine without sources is just an interpreter for
a query language. NebulaStream's source and sink subsystem is what
makes the engine plug into the world — into files, into TCP streams,
into Kafka, into whatever the data is actually flowing through.

The subsystem has four moving parts: **sources** (where bytes come
from), **sinks** (where bytes go to), **input formatters** (how bytes
become tuples) and **output formatters** (how tuples become bytes).
Each is plugin-extensible through a static registry; the engine
shipping today supports a handful of formats out of the box and a
handful more as optional plugins.

This chapter walks through all four parts, with attention to two
non-obvious design choices: the strict separation between source and
formatter, and the *fully-specified descriptor* model that lets
workers run sources without coordinator round-trips.

---

## 8.1 The source contract {#sec-source-contract}

A source's job is to fill a `TupleBuffer` with raw bytes. The
contract is in `nes-sources/include/Sources/Source.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-sources/include/Sources/Source.hpp
class Source {
public:
    class FillTupleBufferResult {
        struct EoS {};
        struct Data { size_t sizeInBytes; };
        std::variant<EoS, Data> result = EoS{};
    public:
        static FillTupleBufferResult eos() { return {}; }
        static FillTupleBufferResult withBytes(size_t sizeInBytes)
            { return FillTupleBufferResult{sizeInBytes}; }
        [[nodiscard]] bool isEoS() const { return std::holds_alternative<EoS>(result); }
        [[nodiscard]] size_t getNumberOfBytes() const
            { return std::get<Data>(result).sizeInBytes; }
    };
    virtual FillTupleBufferResult fillTupleBuffer(TupleBuffer buffer) = 0;
};
```

One method: `fillTupleBuffer`. The buffer is given to the source
empty; the source writes raw bytes into it and returns either
"end of stream" or "I wrote N bytes." That is it.

What this contract does *not* do: the source does not parse the
bytes. A CSV source produces a buffer full of newline-separated
ASCII; a JSON source produces a buffer full of brace-bracketed JSON
text. Neither knows what the schema is. Parsing happens later.

The reason for this separation is throughput. Reading from a TCP
socket and parsing CSV are different work; doing them in different
threads (or, more importantly, on different cores) lets each one
saturate its bottleneck independently. The source thread's
bottleneck is I/O; the formatter thread's bottleneck is CPU. They
should not block each other.

---

## 8.2 The descriptor model {#sec-descriptors}

Every source has two artefacts in the engine:

- A **`SourceDescriptor`**, declared up front by the user and
  resolved by the binder. It is just configuration: type name (e.g.,
  "TCP", "File"), key-value config map, schema.

- A **`Source` implementation**, instantiated at query startup from
  the descriptor by looking up the type name in the source registry.

The descriptor contains everything the engine needs to construct
the source. Critically, this design makes workers stateless with
respect to source configuration: a worker receives the descriptor
embedded in the `CompiledQueryPlan` and constructs its own source
instance, with no need to consult the coordinator at runtime.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 8.1: descriptor for a TCP source"}

```
SourceDescriptor {
    type = "TCP"
    config = {
        "HOST": "vehicle-1.local",
        "PORT": "5001",
        "TIMEOUT_MS": "5000"
    }
    schema = Schema { vehicles$id: UINT64, vehicles$speed: FLOAT64, ... }
    formatter = FormatterDescriptor {
        type = "CSV",
        config = { "TUPLE_DELIMITER": "\n", "FIELD_DELIMITER": "," }
    }
}
```

Worker receives this descriptor, looks up "TCP" in
`SourceRegistry`, constructs a `TCPSource` configured with the
host/port/timeout, and connects. Same for the formatter.
:::

This is one of the design choices documented in the
`docs/design/20240702_sources_and_sinks.md` design document. The
goal stated there is "stateless worker": all per-source state lives
in the descriptor, not on the worker. The motivation is operational:
in a future distributed deployment, queries can be moved between
workers without state migration; only the descriptor moves.

---

## 8.3 The input formatter chain {#sec-input-formatters}

Bytes from a source go to an input formatter. The formatter's job
is to read the raw bytes and produce a *formatted* `TupleBuffer`
whose layout matches the schema.

The formatter splits this into two phases:

**Phase 1 — Indexing.** Walk the raw bytes, find tuple boundaries,
locate field offsets. The output of this phase is a set of indices
(byte offsets) into the raw buffer. No data is copied.

**Phase 2 — Parsing.** Use the indices to read each field's bytes,
convert from the source format (e.g., the ASCII string `"3.14"`)
to the native NebulaStream format (the IEEE-754 `double` value
`3.14`), and write into the formatted buffer.

The split exists because indexing can sometimes be parallelised
(splitting work between threads on tuple boundaries), and because
some sources can perform indexing themselves (a Parquet file source
already has field offsets), in which case the indexing phase is a
no-op.

The interface is in `nes-input-formatters/include/InputFormatters/InputFormatter.hpp`:

```cpp
// nes-input-formatters/include/InputFormatters/InputFormatter.hpp
class InputFormatter {
public:
    virtual void parseTupleBuffer(
        const TupleBuffer& rawBuffer,
        TupleBuffer& formattedBuffer,
        const Schema& schema) = 0;
    // ... index-related methods omitted ...
};
```

The implementations live in `nes-input-formatters/`:

- **`CSVInputFormatter`** — handles the textbook case. Configurable
  field and tuple delimiters.
- **`JSONInputFormatter`** — uses simdjson [@simdjson] for fast
  parsing.
- **`NativeInputFormatter`** — an identity formatter for sources that
  already produce native-format tuples.

Adding a formatter is a registry registration plus a class
implementing the interface. We will see the registry pattern in
Chapter 13.

---

## 8.4 SequenceShredder: tuples that span buffers {#sec-shredder}

A 12 KiB JSON record does not fit in an 8 KiB raw buffer. A 100-line
CSV file followed by a partial 101st line at byte 8190 leaves the
101st line straddling buffer boundary. The formatter has to handle
these cases.

The component that does is the `SequenceShredder`, documented
extensively in `nes-input-formatters/README.md`. The shredder
maintains per-source state about partial tuples and reassembles
them when the missing pieces arrive. It is what allows the
formatter to operate on independent buffers in parallel without
losing tuples that cross boundaries.

The shredder is the reason tuples carry `SequenceNumber` *and*
`ChunkNumber` (Chapter 7): chunks let the shredder know that
sequence number S has multiple physical pieces.

---

## 8.5 Sinks and output formatters {#sec-sinks}

Sinks mirror sources in shape. The interface is in
`nes-sinks/include/Sinks/Sink.hpp`, smaller because sinks have less
work to do:

```cpp
// nes-sinks/include/Sinks/Sink.hpp
class Sink {
public:
    virtual void start(...) = 0;
    virtual void execute(const TupleBuffer& formatted, ...) = 0;
    virtual void stop(...) = 0;
};
```

Each `execute` call receives a formatted `TupleBuffer`. The sink
hands it to its output formatter, which produces the wire-format
bytes, then writes those bytes to the destination (file, TCP
socket, etc.).

Built-in sinks include `FileSink`, `PrintSink`, and (as an optional
plugin) `VoidSink` (for benchmarking — discards everything). Output
formatters mirror the input side: CSV and JSON, with a "Native"
identity case.

The asymmetry between source and sink declarations in SQL (Chapter 5
mentioned this) is reflected here: sinks combine declaration and
implementation in one statement because a single logical sink does
not benefit from multiple physical implementations the way a source
does.

---

## 8.6 The plugin registry {#sec-source-sink-plugins}

Sources, sinks, input formatters and output formatters are all
plugin-registered. The CMake macro `add_plugin` registers an
internal plugin; `add_plugin_as_library` registers an optional one.
Activating an optional plugin is a single line in
`nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt`:

```cmake
// nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt
activate_optional_plugin("Sources/TCPSource" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("Sources/GeneratorSource" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("Sinks/VoidSink" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("InputFormatters/JSONInputFormatter" ON)
activate_optional_plugin("OutputFormatters/JSONOutputFormatter" ON)
if (NES_ENABLES_TESTS)
    activate_optional_plugin("Sinks/ChecksumSink" ON)
endif()
```

The plugins active by default ship a handful of common sources and
sinks; everything else is opt-in. The full mechanism — including
how the plugin classes register themselves at static initialisation
time without falling into the static-initialisation-order fiasco —
is the subject of Chapter 13.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: how Telegraf does this"}
Telegraf, the InfluxData metrics agent, has 300+ source plugins
("inputs" in their terminology), each compiled into the binary
through a similar register-by-name pattern. NebulaStream's plugin
system is small in comparison (a dozen sources today) but
architecturally the same.

The interesting technical difference is that Telegraf's plugins are
Go interfaces with dynamic dispatch, whereas NebulaStream's are
C++ types resolved at compile time. NebulaStream pays for static
linking with a slower build but a faster runtime.
:::

---

## Summary {#sec-ch8-summary}

NebulaStream's source and sink subsystem separates I/O (sources,
sinks) from format conversion (formatters), with each part
plugin-extensible through a static registry. The descriptor-based
configuration model makes workers stateless: a worker receives a
fully-specified `SourceDescriptor` and constructs its own source
instance with no coordinator round-trip. The `SequenceShredder`
handles tuples that span physical buffer boundaries, allowing
parallel parsing of independent buffers. Sinks mirror sources in
shape but combine logical/physical declaration into a single
statement because the multi-physical fan-in pattern that motivates
the source split does not apply on the output side.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch8-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 8.1: build a custom CSV"}
Construct a CSV file with a quoted field containing a newline:

```
1,"hello\nworld",42
2,"good\nbye",99
```

Run a query reading this file. Does NebulaStream handle quoted
multiline fields correctly? If yes, where in the
`CSVInputFormatter` is the quoting logic? If no, what does the
formatter do — drop, error, or split?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 8.2: a TCP source"}
Activate the TCP source plugin (it is on by default but verify
in `nes-plugins/CMakeLists.txt`). Use `netcat` to feed lines into
the worker:

```shell
nc -l 5001 < demo-input.csv
```

… and a query reading from it. Compare the throughput against
the file source. Where is the bottleneck? Hint: it is almost
certainly the TCP buffer, not the engine.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 8.3: trace a multi-chunk record"}
Create a JSON file with one record larger than the default
TupleBuffer (8 KiB). Run a query reading it in TRACE mode. Watch
the chunk numbers in the buffer metadata. The
`SequenceShredder` should reassemble the record before the
windowing/aggregation operators see it. Verify this in the log.
:::
